packet.headline_seed: Second carcass-eating fly species cleared by FDA for maggot wound therapy
packet.description_seed: The Food and Drug Administration this week cleared a second carcass-feasting fly species for use in maggot wound therapy, according to an announcement from Cuprina Holdings , a Singapore-based company that has dubbed its new therapeutic larvae MediFly Maggots. With the clearance, Cuprina appears to be the only company to have FDA clearance to sell two species of fly larvae—and it's abuzz with the potential to dominate the global maggot market. The new species is Lucilia cuprina , or Australian sheep blowfly. It's a close relative of Lucilia sericata , or the common green bottle fly, which is the fly species most often used for wound therapy, often called biosurgery or maggot debridement therapy (MDT). L. sericata is the only other fly with FDA clearance, which the agency first granted in 2004 to Ronald Sherman, who is now Cuprina’s Medical and Scientific Director . Read full article Comments

The Food and Drug Administration this week cleared a second carcass-feasting fly species for use in maggot wound therapy, according to an announcement from Cuprina Holdings, a Singapore-based company that has dubbed its new therapeutic larvae MediFly Maggots. With the clearance, Cuprina appears to be the only company to have FDA clearance to sell two species of fly larvae—and it’s abuzz with the potential to dominate the global maggot market. The new species is Lucilia cuprina, or Australian sheep blowfly. It’s a close relative of Lucilia sericata, or the common green bottle fly, which is the fly species most often used for wound therapy, often called biosurgery or maggot debridement therapy (MDT). L. sericata is the only other fly with FDA clearance, which the agency first granted in 2004 to Ronald Sherman, who is now Cuprina’s Medical and Scientific Director.

For his part, Sherman, a long-time champion of wriggling remedies, cheered the clearance as a step forward for MDT generally. “Maggot debridement therapy has earned its place in modern wound care, and adding a second FDA-cleared species strengthens the entire field,” Sherman said. “Lucilia cuprina has a meaningful international track record, and bring[ing] it under US FDA clearance gives clinicians and their patients more flexibility in how this therapy is delivered.” The idea of allowing baby flies to help clean out wounds dates back centuries, but has yet to be embraced by modern medicine—for various reasons. The most obvious is the “ick” factor, which zaps enthusiasm from both patients and healthcare providers. This has led some larvae lovers to push for a rebrand, such as reframing larvae as adorable newborn flies, wee walruses, or maggies.

“We now hold FDA clearance for both species used in MDT, a position no other company holds,” Cuprina CEO David Quek said in a statement. “This anchors our wound-care platform in one of the world’s most demanding regulatory markets and gives us a defensible edge as we continue to build our portfolio.” The company makes no claims of any significant therapeutic difference between the two maggot treatments. Rather, they are seen as fitting into different markets. L. sericata is more familiar in Western wound care, Cuprina says, while L. cuprina may have more recognition in Australia, Africa, Asia, and parts of the Americas.

payload.title: FDA hyväksyi toisen kärpäslajin toukat haavojen puhdistushoitoon
payload.summary: Yhdysvaltain elintarvike- ja lääkevirasto FDA on hyväksynyt Lucilia cuprina -kärpäsen toukat käytettäväksi toukkahoidossa, jossa haavoista poistetaan kuollutta kudosta. Hyväksyntä vahvistaa singaporelaisen Cuprinan asemaa erikoistuneessa haavanhoidossa.
payload.content:
Yhdysvaltain elintarvike- ja lääkevirasto FDA on hyväksynyt toisen kärpäslajin käytettäväksi toukkahoidossa, jossa elävät toukat auttavat puhdistamaan haavoja kuolleesta kudoksesta. Uusi hyväksytty laji on Lucilia cuprina, joka tunnetaan myös Australian sheep blowfly -nimellä, ja sitä markkinoi singaporelainen Cuprina Holdings.

## Toinen FDA:n hyväksymä laji

Toukkahoitoa kutsutaan myös biosurgiaksi tai maggot debridement therapy -hoidoksi. Menetelmässä kärpäsen toukkia käytetään haavojen puhdistamiseen tilanteissa, joissa kuollut kudos täytyy poistaa paranemisen edistämiseksi. Lähdeaineiston mukaan FDA:n hyväksyntä koskee Cuprinan MediFly Maggots -nimellä tarjoamia terapeuttisia toukkia.

Lucilia cuprina on läheistä sukua Lucilia sericata -lajille, joka on tavallisemmin käytetty kärpäslaji haavanhoidossa. Lucilia sericata oli aiemmin ainoa FDA:n hyväksymä laji tähän käyttöön. Ensimmäinen hyväksyntä myönnettiin vuonna 2004 Ronald Shermanille, joka toimii nykyisin Cuprinan lääketieteellisenä ja tieteellisenä johtajana.

Shermanin mukaan toisen FDA:n hyväksymän lajin lisääminen vahvistaa koko hoitomuodon asemaa. Hänen mukaansa Lucilia cuprinalla on kansainvälistä käyttöhistoriaa, ja sen hyväksyminen Yhdysvaltain sääntelykehyksessä antaa lääkäreille ja potilaille lisää joustoa hoidon toteuttamiseen.

## Cuprina hakee asemaa erikoismarkkinassa

Cuprina näyttää hyväksynnän jälkeen olevan ainoa yhtiö, jolla on FDA:n hyväksyntä kahden toukkahoidossa käytettävän kärpäslajin myyntiin. Yhtiön toimitusjohtaja David Quek kuvasi asemaa merkittäväksi haavanhoitoalustan rakentamisessa, koska Yhdysvaltain viranomaisympäristöä pidetään yhtenä maailman vaativimmista.

Yhtiö ei kuitenkaan väitä, että kahden toukkahoidon välillä olisi merkittävä terapeuttinen ero. Sen sijaan lajit nähdään osin eri markkinoille sopivina. Cuprinan mukaan Lucilia sericata tunnetaan paremmin länsimaisessa haavanhoidossa, kun taas Lucilia cuprina voi olla tutumpi Australiassa, Afrikassa, Aasiassa ja osissa Amerikkaa.

Toukkahoidolla on pitkä historia, mutta se ei ole noussut modernin lääketieteen valtavirtaan. Yksi ilmeinen este on hoidon herättämä vastenmielisyys sekä potilaissa että terveydenhuollon ammattilaisissa. FDA:n uusi hyväksyntä ei yksin ratkaise tätä mielikuvahaastetta, mutta se laajentaa virallisesti hyväksyttyjen vaihtoehtojen joukkoa pienellä ja erikoistuneella haavanhoidon alueella.
summary_bullets: FDA hyväksyi Lucilia cuprina -kärpäsen toukat käytettäväksi haavojen toukkahoidossa.
Cuprina näyttää olevan ainoa yhtiö, jolla on FDA:n hyväksyntä kahdelle toukkahoidossa käytettävälle kärpäslajille.
Yhtiö ei väitä uuden lajin olevan merkittävästi tehokkaampi, vaan näkee lajien sopivan eri markkinoille.

article.title: FDA hyväksyi toisen kärpäslajin toukat haavojen puhdistushoitoon
article.description: Yhdysvaltain elintarvike- ja lääkevirasto FDA on hyväksynyt Lucilia cuprina -kärpäsen toukat käytettäväksi toukkahoidossa, jossa haavoista poistetaan kuollutta kudosta. Hyväksyntä vahvistaa singaporelaisen Cuprinan asemaa erikoistuneessa haavanhoidossa.

[Lähde: Ars Technica]
The Food and Drug Administration this week cleared a second carcass-feasting fly species for use in maggot wound therapy, according to an announcement from Cuprina Holdings, a Singapore-based company that has dubbed its new therapeutic larvae MediFly Maggots.

With the clearance, Cuprina appears to be the only company to have FDA clearance to sell two species of fly larvae—and it’s abuzz with the potential to dominate the global maggot market.

The new species is Lucilia cuprina, or Australian sheep blowfly. It’s a close relative of Lucilia sericata, or the common green bottle fly, which is the fly species most often used for wound therapy, often called biosurgery or maggot debridement therapy (MDT). L. sericata is the only other fly with FDA clearance, which the agency first granted in 2004 to Ronald Sherman, who is now Cuprina’s Medical and Scientific Director.

The company makes no claims of any significant therapeutic difference between the two maggot treatments. Rather, they are seen as fitting into different markets. L. sericata is more familiar in Western wound care, Cuprina says, while L. cuprina may have more recognition in Australia, Africa, Asia, and parts of the Americas.

For his part, Sherman, a long-time champion of wriggling remedies, cheered the clearance as a step forward for MDT generally. “Maggot debridement therapy has earned its place in modern wound care, and adding a second FDA-cleared species strengthens the entire field,” Sherman said. “Lucilia cuprina has a meaningful international track record, and bring[ing] it under US FDA clearance gives clinicians and their patients more flexibility in how this therapy is delivered.”

With the clearance, Cuprina appears to be the only company to have FDA clearance to sell two species of fly larvae—and it’s abuzz with the potential to dominate the global maggot market. The new species is Lucilia cuprina, or Australian sheep blowfly. It’s a close relative of Lucilia sericata, or the common green bottle fly, which is the fly species most often used for wound therapy, often called biosurgery or maggot debridement therapy (MDT). L. sericata is the only other fly with FDA clearance, which the agency first granted in 2004 to Ronald Sherman, who is now Cuprina’s Medical and Scientific Director.

For his part, Sherman, a long-time champion of wriggling remedies, cheered the clearance as a step forward for MDT generally. “Maggot debridement therapy has earned its place in modern wound care, and adding a second FDA-cleared species strengthens the entire field,” Sherman said. “Lucilia cuprina has a meaningful international track record, and bring[ing] it under US FDA clearance gives clinicians and their patients more flexibility in how this therapy is delivered.” The idea of allowing baby flies to help clean out wounds dates back centuries, but has yet to be embraced by modern medicine—for various reasons. The most obvious is the “ick” factor, which zaps enthusiasm from both patients and healthcare providers. This has led some larvae lovers to push for a rebrand, such as reframing larvae as adorable newborn flies, wee walruses, or maggies.

“We now hold FDA clearance for both species used in MDT, a position no other company holds,” Cuprina CEO David Quek said in a statement. “This anchors our wound-care platform in one of the world’s most demanding regulatory markets and gives us a defensible edge as we continue to build our portfolio.” The company makes no claims of any significant therapeutic difference between the two maggot treatments. Rather, they are seen as fitting into different markets. L. sericata is more familiar in Western wound care, Cuprina says, while L. cuprina may have more recognition in Australia, Africa, Asia, and parts of the Americas.
